homeland.en: The Syrian steppe and the middle Euphrates; people with Amorite names are recorded in Middle Bronze Age Canaan, and a later kingdom called Amurru lay in the mountains and coast of northern Lebanon.

summary.en: "Amorites" is the name Sumerian and Akkadian texts of about 2400-1600 BCE gave to West Semitic-speaking groups from "the West" (Gottwald, Encyclopaedia Judaica). Egyptian Execration Texts of the 20th-19th centuries BCE show people with such names in Palestine. There is no evidence that they called themselves Amorites. The Hebrew Bible later uses "Amorite" for pre-Israelite inhabitants of the land, a usage scholars cannot tie directly to the earlier term.

The Hebrew Bible uses "Amorite" both for all pre-Israelite inhabitants and for one group among them (textual tradition). Irfan Shahid (2009) counts the "Ammorites" among waves of Semitic migration from the Arabian peninsula; see the canaanites record for that debate.

homeland.en: Late Bronze Age Canaan: most of Palestine west of the Jordan and the Lebanese-Syrian coast, organised in city-states such as Hazor, Megiddo, Shechem, Jerusalem and Gezer.

summary.en: The Bronze Age population of Canaan, named as such in 15th-14th-century BCE texts from Egypt, Syria and northern Mesopotamia and known archaeologically from shared material culture. Ancient DNA from nine sites in Israel, Jordan and Lebanon shows that people of this "Canaanite" culture were genetically similar to one another and descended from earlier local Neolithic populations mixed with Zagros/Caucasus-related newcomers (Agranat-Tamir et al. 2020; Haber et al. 2017). After about 1200 BCE the coastal Canaanites are usually called Phoenicians; inland, Canaanite populations became part of the Iron Age kingdoms.

notes.en: Origins are described differently by evidence type. Genetic studies (Haber 2017; Agranat-Tamir 2020) model Bronze Age Canaanite ancestry as local Neolithic plus Zagros/Caucasus-related gene flow, and find a "Canaanite-related" component in present-day Levantine groups; Agranat-Tamir et al. stress that this "does not mean" direct descent and that genetics cannot prove past identities (linking these findings to present-day groups is left to the 640-today records). Dahood (New Catholic Encyclopedia) dates Canaanite settlement to before 3000 BCE from place names. A view common in Arab historiography, stated for example by Abu Hatab and Abbas (2022, in Arabic; our translation: "the Canaanites are one of the tribes that migrated from the Arabian peninsula and settled Palestine in the third millennium BCE") and by Shahid (2009), derives them from Semitic migrations out of Arabia. Hurrian personal names among Late Bronze Age rulers point to northern elements. The Bible lists Jebusites, Hivites, Girgashites and others among the "sons of Canaan" (textual tradition; Gen 10). Dahood's view that "Canaanite" and "Phoenician" name the same people before and after 1200 BCE is followed in the link to phoenicians.

summary.en: Rulers of Levantine origin who governed northern Egypt as the 15th Dynasty (c. 1640-1530 BCE) from Avaris, together with the Levantine-derived population of the eastern Delta. Isotope evidence suggests their ancestors had immigrated over centuries rather than invading (Stantis et al. 2020). Ahmose I expelled them and besieged their last stronghold, Sharuhen in southern Canaan.

Textual tradition: Manetho (3rd century BCE, quoted by Josephus) told of an invasion and of the expelled "shepherds" founding Jerusalem; Josephus identified them with the ancestors of the Jews. Modern scholars treat this as tradition: Redford (via EJ) sees at most distant memories behind the exodus story, and Thompson calls Hyksos rule mainly an internal Egyptian development whose links to Palestine were secondary.

summary.en: An Egyptian term, used from the 18th Dynasty into the Third Intermediate Period, for pastoral nomads on the edges of Canaan (Kennedy). Egyptian texts place Shasu in southern Transjordan, including Shasu tribes of Edom whom frontier officials let into the Delta to pasture their herds under Merneptah (Papyrus Anastasi VI). Archaeologists such as Kafafi and Killebrew see such pastoralists as one source of the Iron Age peoples of Transjordan and of early Israel.

summary.en: Documentary evidence first names "Israel" as a people in Canaan on Merneptah's stela (late 13th century BCE); Assyrian texts later name Ahab "the Israelite" (853 BCE). Archaeology traces an Iron I wave of hill-country villages that continued into the kingdoms of Israel and Judah. The biblical account (textual tradition) instead tells of descent from the patriarchs, an exodus from Egypt and a conquest of Canaan. The northern kingdom ended with the Assyrian conquest of 722-720 BCE.

notes.en: Keep evidence apart: (1) documentary - Merneptah Stela (c. 1208 BCE), Mesha Stela and Assyrian annals (9th-8th centuries); (2) archaeological - Iron I highland villages, which Finkelstein labels "Israelite" because they continue into the kingdoms; (3) textual tradition - patriarchs, exodus, conquest and the twelve tribes, whose historicity is debated (Dever: no direct proof for Abraham; Thompson doubts that Judah, Samaria and Galilee had a single origin). Origin debates are recorded as links from canaanites, shasu and apiru. Dates are given for the documented people; the name "Israel" was later taken up in Judah as a religious and national name (Finkelstein, ch. 7).

summary.en: The people of the kingdom of Judah, named in Assyrian inscriptions from the 730s BCE (biblical tradition traces them to the tribe of Judah and the house of David). After the Babylonian conquests of 597-582 BCE part of the population was deported to Babylonia and some fled to Egypt, while others stayed in the land. These groups are the root of the later Judeans (Jews) of the Persian period and the diaspora.

summary.en: After the Assyrian conquest of 722-720 BCE the province of Samaria was home to the Israelites who remained and to groups the Assyrians brought in from Babylonia, Hamath and Arabia. Assyrian records call deportees from here "Samarians" (Radner). The province continued under Babylonian and Persian rule; Judean returnees treated its people as outsiders (Ezra 4).

summary.en: A people first named in Egyptian records of Ramesses III among the "Sea Peoples", who settled the southern coast early in the Iron Age with an Aegean-related material culture. Ancient DNA from Ashkelon shows newcomers with European-related ancestry whose genetic trace faded within two centuries (Feldman et al. 2019). Their cities lived on under Assyrian rule until the Babylonian conquest of 604 BCE, after which the Philistines no longer appear as a distinct people.

How much of the Philistine population came from outside is debated (Killebrew via Barrick; Maeir and others stress entangled identities; see the migration philistine-arrival). The Palestinian historian Nur Masalha, as summarised by Al Aqad (2025), treats Philistia as a distinct entity and argues for continuity between Philistia and later Palestinian identities; Greenfield and Sperling (EJ) hold that after the Babylonian conquest only the territorial name Palestine linked the coastal cities to their Philistine past.

summary.en: The Iron Age name for the Canaanites of the Lebanese coast, organised in city-states such as Tyre and Sidon. They traded and founded colonies across the Mediterranean, spread the alphabet, and kept their language on the mainland through the Persian and Hellenistic periods, until about the 1st century BCE (Gzella).

Assyria annexed the Aramean states in the 8th century BCE and moved many Arameans across its empire. As a people they faded, but their language became the common tongue of the Near East and was adopted by Judeans and others.

Jordanian excavations show continuity from the Late Bronze Age and dense settlement into the Persian period (Kafafi). After Babylonian rule Ammon became a province; how far its people kept a separate identity is debated.

Moab was a vassal of Assyria and Babylonia; after a Babylonian campaign in 582 BCE it disappears as a kingdom, and Oded (EJ) holds that the Moabites who stayed were absorbed by incoming Arab tribes.

summary.en: The people of Judah after the Babylonian exile, named after the land of Judah (Yehud, Judaea) and centred on the Jerusalem temple until 70 CE. Documents from the Persian period onwards call them Jews or Judeans, both in the land and in a growing diaspora (Elephantine, Alexandria, Babylonia, Rome). After the revolts against Rome (66-73 and 132-135 CE) their centre in the land moved to Galilee; the people continues to the present.

notes.en: Start date: the record begins with the Persian period by the division of this research (Judahites before 539 BCE belong to the Iron Age group); the Hebrew name Yehudi is older. Terminology is debated: the Greek Ioudaios can be rendered 'Judean' (a people of a land) or 'Jew' (a member of a religious community); scholars such as Seth Schwartz (as summarised by Gibson, BMCR 2002.09.36) see Herod as turning 'Judaean institutions into Jewish ones', and recent studies use 'Judeans' for the earlier period (Kraemer, BMCR 2022.09.04). Schwartz's further thesis that after 135 CE many Jews in Palestine 'may have come to forget Judaism' is a minority, provocative view (as the reviewer notes); archaeology in Galilee shows continued Jewish settlement (Raviv and Ben David 2021). Eusebius' Onomasticon (early 4th century) still lists 'large villages of Jews' in the southern Hebron hills (Daroma). Genetic studies of present-day Jewish groups belong to the period from 640 CE (group P3).

summary.en: An ethno-religious community centred on Mount Gerizim that holds the Five Books of Moses and regards itself as the descendants of the Israelites of the northern kingdom. It became distinct from the Jews of Judea during the Persian and Hellenistic periods; its temple on Gerizim was destroyed by John Hyrcanus in the late 2nd century BCE. Revolts against Byzantine rule in the 5th-6th centuries and forced conversions sharply reduced the community, which survives today near Nablus and in Holon.

summary.en: The mixed population of the region south of Judea in the Persian and Hellenistic periods, descended largely from Edomites who had moved west of the Arabah, together with Qedarite and other Arabs, Judahites and others; its main deity was Qaus. The district of Idumea is first named in accounts of 312 BCE. Conquered by John Hyrcanus I in the late 2nd century BCE, the Idumeans were incorporated into the Jewish people; Herod the Great came from an Idumean family, and Idumeans last appear as a distinct group in the war against Rome (66-70 CE).

Greek and Roman authors described them as mountain robbers and archers; recent studies argue that they were a settled local population with organised rule from about 200 BCE. Their territory was absorbed into the Roman province of Syria and the Herodian kingdoms in the 1st century CE, while Iturean archer units served in the Roman army.

First described in Greek accounts of 312 BCE, they wrote in Aramaic but bore Arabic names. Rome annexed their kingdom in 106 CE as the province of Arabia; Nabataean inscriptions and culture continued into the Roman period, and the Nabataean script developed into the Arabic script.

summary.en: The civic communities of the Greek-style cities founded or refounded after Alexander's conquest: Macedonian and Greek settlers and veterans, and local Phoenicians, Philistine-coast townspeople, Idumeans, Syrians and Arabs who took up Greek language and institutions. Jewish sources call them Greeks or Syrians. Several were taken over by the Hasmoneans and restored by Pompey in 63 BCE; Hadrian settled non-Jewish colonists at Aelia Capitolina. Most became Christian between the 4th and 6th centuries, while some cities, such as Gaza, kept their temples late.

summary.en: The followers of Jesus of Nazareth, a movement that began among Jews in Judea and Galilee in the 1st century CE and spread to non-Jews. After Constantine (from 313) the land became a Christian holy land of churches, monasteries and pilgrimage, and by the 6th century most of the population of Palestine and Arabia was Christian, drawn from converted townspeople, villagers, Samaritans, Nabataeans and Arab tribes. Christians remained the majority for several centuries after the Arab conquest, and the community continues today.

The Jafnids were Miaphysite Christians and patrons of churches and monasteries. Their power declined after 580; their last ruler, Jabala ibn al-Ayham, fought for Byzantium at the Yarmuk (636) and then left for Byzantine territory, while other Ghassanids joined the new Muslim order.

Rome and Byzantium employed successive tribal confederations (Tanukh, then Salih, then Ghassan) as allied 'phylarchs'; many tribesmen became Christians from the 4th century. Tribes such as Lakhm and Judham lived in southern Palestine and Transjordan before Islam and became part of the Arab population of the early Islamic provinces.

Historians agree that the change was gradual but disagree on its pace and on how much of it came from conversion of the existing population rather than from settlement of newcomers. By the sixteenth century, Ottoman records show a mostly Muslim population, with Christian, Jewish and other minorities.

label.en: Babylonia: Babylon and the Nippur countryside, including Al-Yahudu ("Judah-town")

summary.en: The Babylonian Chronicle records Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Jerusalem in 597 BCE; 2 Kings and Jeremiah record deportations in 597, 586 and 582 BCE. Babylonian tablets name the exiled king Jehoiachin and, from 572 BCE, a "town of Judah" in the countryside; the deportees farmed state land, and many stayed after the Persian conquest (Alstola).

notes.en: Numbers of deportees differ between 2 Kings and Jeremiah (see the migration babylonian-exile). The Babylonian Jewish community that grew from these deportees is followed in the 539 BCE-640 CE and later records.

label.en: Egypt: Tahpanhes, Migdol and Memphis in the north; later the Judean garrison at Elephantine in the south

summary.en: According to 2 Kings and Jeremiah (textual tradition), after the murder of the governor Gedaliah many Judahites fled to Egypt, settling in Tahpanhes, Migdol, Memphis and Pathros. Documentary evidence of Judeans in Egypt comes from the 5th century BCE, when part of the soldiers at Elephantine were of Judean origin (Alstola).

label.en: Babylonia (Babylon and a settlement named after Ashkelon in the Nippur countryside)

summary.en: The Babylonian Chronicle records Nebuchadnezzar's capture of Ashkelon and its king in late 604 BCE. Babylonian lists name the kings of Gaza and Ashdod and princes of Ashkelon, and a place named Ashkelon appears among deportee settlements in the Babylonian countryside (EJ; Alstola).

label.en: Mixed population of the Persian- and Hellenistic-period coastal cities (Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod)

summary.en: After 604 BCE the remaining people of Philistia merged into the mixed population of the Persian- and Hellenistic-period coastal cities (Greenfield and Sperling, EJ). Nehemiah (textual tradition, 5th century BCE) still speaks of an "Ashdodite" language. Masalha, as reviewed by Al Aqad, argues for continuity from Philistia to later Palestinian identities.

Contested on the question of continuity of identity, not on the fact of a mixed population; Masalha's book itself was not opened (cited via the review). Genetic studies of Iron Age II Ashkelon show the population by then was close to other local Levantines (Feldman et al. 2019, cited in the canaanites--contributed-to--philistines link).

label.en: Phoenician colonies in Cyprus, Sicily, Sardinia, North Africa (Carthage) and Spain

summary.en: From the 11th-10th centuries BCE Phoenician traders set up colonies around the Mediterranean (Dahood); Carthage, founded from Tyre, became the centre of a Punic world whose language survived into the 5th century CE (Gzella).

notes.en: Hamath was of neo-Hittite foundation with a growing Aramaic element (EJ), so "Aramean" is approximate for its people. The Hamath-to-Samaria move itself is known from 2 Kings; Radner reconstructs its context from Assyrian sources.

summary.en: Biblical tradition presents Israel's ancestors as Arameans ("My father was a fugitive Aramean"), and a view reported in the Turkish TDV encyclopedia (after the historian Günaltay) holds that the Hebrews were kin to, or part of, the Arameans and adopted a Canaanite dialect in Canaan. Malamat (EJ) rejects the Aramean affiliation of the patriarchs as an anachronism, since Arameans are not attested before the late 2nd millennium BCE.

label.en: Egypt (Alexandria and the Egyptian countryside; Leontopolis)

summary.en: Under the early Ptolemies large numbers of Jews were taken or went to Egypt, where Alexandria became the largest Jewish centre outside the land. Josephus describes both captives taken by Ptolemy I and voluntary emigrants; the Israeli historian Bezalel Bar-Kochva argues that the main move was a forced deportation that later Jewish writers recast as an emigration.

label.en: Mediterranean diaspora (Rome and other cities of the Roman Empire)

summary.en: After the revolts against Rome many Jews were enslaved or left the land, and the diaspora became the larger part of the Jewish people. Scholars disagree on how far the diaspora was created by these events: reference works stress the exile after 70 CE, while others note that diaspora Jews already outnumbered those in the land before 70 and that a large Jewish population remained in Judea until the Bar Kokhba revolt and in Galilee afterwards.

summary.en: How the Samaritans arose is disputed. Samaritan tradition holds that they are the Israelites of the north who remained in the land; the Bible (2 Kings 17) and Josephus describe them as descendants of foreign settlers brought by the Assyrians ('Cutheans'); many modern historians see both Jews and Samaritans as heirs of the Israelites who separated gradually between the exile and the Hasmonean destruction of the Gerizim temple. A small Y-chromosome study (2013) found Samaritan men closely related to Jewish priestly lineages, which its authors read as support for the Samaritan view.

summary.en: After John Hyrcanus I conquered Idumea (c. 112-107 BCE), the Idumeans were incorporated into the Jewish people. Josephus says they were made to accept circumcision and Jewish law as a condition of staying in their land; Strabo describes them joining the Judeans without mentioning force, and many modern scholars doubt forced conversion and stress the Idumeans' rapid integration.

summary.en: The Karaite movement grew out of dissident trends among the Jews of Babylonia and Persia; its precursors, the Ananites, were named after Anan ben David, and the name Karaites appears in the ninth century (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

sources.quote: The name "Karaites" was not applied to the sect until the ninth century; the precursor of the sect was known as "Ananites," from the name of its founder

summary.en: After 1948 the Karaites of Egypt and Iraq left for Israel, mainly after the Suez crisis of 1956 and in 1962, settling first around Ramla (Encyclopaedia Judaica).

sources.quote: caused the Karaites in Egypt and Iraq to settle in Israel
They first settled mainly in the Ramleh area and from there spread to other areas.

summary.en: In the war of 1947-1949 most Palestinian Arabs of the areas that became Israel left their homes and became refugees. The Palestinian historian Maher Charif writes that they were forced out by Jewish forces; Israel's foreign ministry holds that Arab leaders encouraged the flight and that in places such as Haifa Jewish authorities asked Arabs to stay; Muslih describes both expulsion and flight out of fear.

sources.quote: In 1948, three-quarters of a million Palestinians were forced to leave their land and country
The Arab leadership encouraged and even instigated this mass exodus of the Arab civilian population
In some places, notably in Haifa, the Jewish authorities pleaded with the panic-stricken Arabs not to leave, but their efforts were in vain.
many of them forcefully expelled by the Jewish forces while others fled out of fear

notes.en: See the perspectives topic causes-of-1948-exodus for the full debate (Morris, Khalidi, Karsh and others). No casualty figures are given here.

label.en: Jordan (East Bank)

summary.en: Refugees of 1948 went to Jordan and to the West Bank, which Jordan annexed, and a second wave crossed to the East Bank in 1967 (Hovsepian).

sources.quote: into the nearby Arab countries of Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria, as well as into the West Bank and the Gaza Strip
Al Naksa created an additional 350,000 refugees who fled to Jordan

label.en: Lebanon

summary.en: Refugees from Galilee and the northern coast went to Lebanon; Charif describes Haifa's remaining Arab residents leaving by sea for Lebanon in April 1948 (Hovsepian; Charif).

sources.quote: into the nearby Arab countries of Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria, as well as into the West Bank and the Gaza Strip
they sailed to Lebanon

label.en: Syria

summary.en: Refugees from northern and eastern Galilee went to Syria (Hovsepian); the Algerian community of Galilee was among them (Yannis Arab).

sources.quote: into the nearby Arab countries of Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria, as well as into the West Bank and the Gaza Strip
they were forcibly expelled by Zionist forces to Syria

summary.en: The refugees of 1948 and 1967 and their descendants form the core of the Palestinian diaspora, which Muslih counts as the majority of the people after 1948 and the Palestinian statistics bureau still counts as larger than the population in Palestine.

sources.quote: Uprooted, dispersed, and with no state of their own, diaspora Palestinians (60% of the Palestinian population in 1948) came under the guardianship of the host Arab countries in which they lived.
This continued dispersal underscores the long-term political and historical drivers of forced displacement.

summary.en: The Palestinians who stayed in the territory of Israel in 1948-1949 became its Arab citizens under military rule (to 1966); the Nationality Law of 1952 set the terms of their citizenship (Masri; Hovsepian).

sources.quote: Palestinians who remained in their homeland found themselves under the control of a new regime: Israel.
It enacted the Nationality Law of 1952
The indigenous Palestinian population that remained on the land under Israeli control was put under military rule until 1966

summary.en: The Bedouin who remained in the Negev and Galilee after 1948 became Israeli citizens; Ahmad Amara describes their long struggle over land and unrecognised villages, while Frantzman, Yahel and Kark stress Israel's efforts to integrate them.

sources.quote: is representative of Palestinian Bedouin communities that have been engaged in a struggle with the Israeli government over land ownership and housing rights since 1948.
attempts have been made since the beginnings of the modern state to incorporate and integrate them into Israel’s multiethnic society

summary.en: The Druze of Galilee and Carmel are Israeli citizens and are counted among the country's Arab communities, but their place in it is contested: Britannica stresses their loyalty to the state and military service, while the Palestinian legal scholar Mazen Masri sees the separate treatment of Druze as part of a policy of dividing the Palestinian citizens into 'minorities'.

sources.quote: They are the only Arab group conscripted into the Israel Defense Forces
to promote narrower sectarian identities recasting the Palestinians as “the minorities”: an amalgam of Muslim, Christian, Druze and Bedouin communities with no uniting identity
except members of the Druze community who nevertheless have not enjoyed equal rights or treatment as the Jews

notes.en: The Druze of the Golan Heights mostly regard themselves as Syrian citizens and are not part of this link.
